paragraphs.text: Madia et al. (2008) described benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME or FAME) as an autosomal dominant condition characterized by shivering-like tremors of cortical origin, myoclonus, and epilepsy. De Fusco et al. (2014) described autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME) as a familial disorder with cortical reflex myoclonus. It presents as action-induced shivering movements of the hands and jerking of the upper limbs, variably associated with focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures of variable severity. A minority of patients have borderline or moderately impaired cognition, and myoclonus often worsens in advanced age.

paragraphs.text: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree in which 8 individuals had a nonprogressive disorder with onset between 12 and 50 years of age. All had mainly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most rarely had seizures and had normal cognition, but 3 individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All patients had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Neurophysiologic studies showed that the myoclonus was cortical in origin. In 5 patients, EEG over the contralateral rolandic area was coherent with EMG at 8 to 25 Hz, and EEG activity preceded EMG activity by 8 to 15 ms; ipsilateral coherence in 2 patients was consistent with transcallosal spread. Patients had an enhanced C-reflex and high-amplitude somatosensory and visual evoked potentials. Compared with controls, they had a reduced resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation and a shortened post-MEP silent period. Guerrini et al. (2001) suggested that these findings reflected diffuse cortical hyperexcitability.

paragraphs.text: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean, 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members. Three presymptomatic members had giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long loop reflex I; after 1.5 years of follow-up, these members developed hand tremor and myoclonus of the upper limbs.

paragraphs.text: Suppa et al. (2009) described an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy (FCMTE). Clinically affected family members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neuropsychological testing showed visuospatial impairment, which the authors suggested may be due to temporal lobe dysfunction. Neurophysiologic studies suggested increased excitability of the primary motor cortex with normal sensorimotor integration.

paragraphs.text: Crompton et al. (2012) described a 6-generation kindred of European descent, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia, with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy. All 55 affected family members had fine hand tremor, usually beginning in adolescence (median age 15 years; range 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%) and began later than the hand tremor (median age 17 years; range 5-60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range 18-76 years). Neurophysiologic testing showed features of cortical reflex myoclonus. Crompton et al. (2012) concluded that the most common phenotype in this family was a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, together with subtle proximal myoclonus; generalized tonic-clonic seizures were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset after severe generalized myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) described a 4-generation Tuscan family (family B) with 5 affected members. All had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs, and cortical tremor was the presenting symptom, starting between ages 18 and 50 years. All but one (IV:1) had epilepsy with rare generalized tonic-clonic seizures, at times triggered by visual stimuli; 2 patients also had drug-resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures. One patient had borderline cognitive level and the others had normal intelligence. Jerk-locked back-averaged EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, and long-loop reflex studies were consistent with cortical reflex myoclonus. Brain MRI was normal where performed.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) summarized the clinical features of 22 FAME families. The families were mainly Italian; others were Australian/New Zealand, Sephardic Jewish (Iraqi and Israeli), South African, French/Spanish, French, and Syrian. Patients had cortical myoclonic tremor and myoclonic and later generalized tonic-clonic seizures, with onset usually in the second to third decade. Expressivity varied within and between families, and the frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures ranged from 15% to 100% across families. Some families also had focal seizures. In a large Australian/New Zealand family of European ancestry (Family 1) with 55 affected members, all 55 had myoclonus/cortical tremor, 8 (15%) had tonic-clonic seizures, and 2 (4%) had focal seizures; mean age of onset was 18.6 years, with a range of 4 to 60 years.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a 5-generation Tuscan family (family A) with autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy, De Fusco et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG), resulting in replacement of 5 amino acids (HGGAL) in the third intracellular loop with 4 new residues (QFGR) (p.H225_L229delinsQFGR). The variant was found by candidate gene sequencing, segregated completely with the disease, and was absent from 575 Tuscan controls, dbSNP, the Exome Variant Server, and 1000 Genomes; targeted capture and next-generation sequencing of the critical region in 2 affected members found it to be the only relevant change. The same indel was found in a second Tuscan family (family B) that shared the disease haplotype across the entire chromosome 2 critical region. In transfected HeLa cells, the mutant protein localized normally to the plasma membrane and was internalized to endosomes in an arrestin-dependent manner after epinephrine stimulation; molecular modeling predicted that the change alters the conformation of the third intracellular loop.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 3 FAME families (Families 1, 3, and 19), Corbett et al. (2019) identified, by analysis of whole-genome sequencing data with ExpansionHunter and exSTRa, an expansion of an ATTTT repeat together with an inserted ATTTC repeat within the first intron of the STARD7 gene; the ATTTC repeat was absent from WGS data on 69 controls. By repeat-primed PCR, the ATTTC expansion was found in all 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families, in all 20 affected individuals from 6 additional multiplex families, and in 1 of 52 unrelated singleton cases (158 of 158 typically affected individuals from 22 families), but not in 28 controls. Long-read sequencing showed a forward-strand structure of (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n; one patient from Family 1 had a SMRT read with 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats and a nanopore read with 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats, which the authors suggested reflected somatic variation, and a patient from Family 5 had 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats, 4645 bp in total. Patient fibroblasts showed no change in STARD7 mRNA or protein levels.

checks.claim: In affected members of 3 FAME families (Families 1, 3, and 19), Corbett et al. (2019) identified an expansion of an ATTTT repeat together with an inserted ATTTC repeat within the first intron of the STARD7 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: This revealed an expansion of an ATTTT repeat and insertion of an ATTTC repeat in the context of the reverse strand of chr2 within the first intron of STARD7 (StAR-related lipid transfer domain-containing 7) in all FAME samples tested
checks.explanation: The samples came from Families 1, 3 and 19.

checks.claim: The STARD7 intronic repeat expansion was identified by analysis of whole-genome sequencing data with ExpansionHunter and exSTRa.
checks.evidence_quote: with two repeat expansion detection methods, ExpansionHunter and exSTRa,, to look for similar combined ATTTT and ATTTC repeat expansions

checks.claim: The STARD7 ATTTC repeat was absent from whole-genome sequencing data on 69 controls.
checks.evidence_quote: The ATTTC repeat was not present in any whole-genome sequencing data from 69 control samples

checks.claim: By repeat-primed PCR, the STARD7 ATTTC expansion was found in all 137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families.
checks.evidence_quote: We developed a repeat-primed PCR (RP-PCR) assay to rapidly identify the expansion in 137/137 affected individuals from 16 independently reported FAME2 families worldwide

checks.claim: By repeat-primed PCR, the STARD7 ATTTC expansion was found in all 20 affected individuals from 6 additional multiplex FAME families.
checks.evidence_quote: Of these, 20/20 familial and 1/52 singleton cases were positive for an ATTTC expansion in STARD7
checks.explanation: The 20 cases came from six multiplex families.

checks.claim: By repeat-primed PCR, the STARD7 ATTTC expansion was found in 1 of 52 unrelated singleton cases.
checks.evidence_quote: Of these, 20/20 familial and 1/52 singleton cases were positive for an ATTTC expansion in STARD7

checks.claim: The STARD7 ATTTC expansion was found in 158 of 158 typically affected individuals from 22 families.
checks.evidence_quote: The ATTTC expansions segregate in 158/158 individuals typically affected by FAME from 22 pedigrees

checks.claim: The STARD7 ATTTC expansion was not found in 28 controls.
checks.evidence_quote: The ATTTC repeat expansion did not amplify in any of 28 control DNA samples extracted from unaffected individuals unrelated to FAME.

checks.claim: Long-read sequencing showed that the STARD7 expansion has a forward-strand structure of (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n.
checks.evidence_quote: This suggested the structure of the pathogenic repeat in the context of the forward strand of chr2 was (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n
checks.explanation: The paper inferred this structure from the RP-PCR priming pattern, not from long-read sequencing. Long-read sequencing then gave the repeat counts.

checks.claim: One patient from Family 1 had a SMRT read with 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats in STARD7.
checks.evidence_quote: The SMRT read generated to 99% base accuracy by circular consensus calling was comprised of four subreads and contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats

checks.claim: The same patient from Family 1 had a nanopore read with 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats in STARD7.
checks.evidence_quote: The Oxford Nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats with some interruptions

checks.claim: Corbett et al. (2019) suggested that the differing SMRT and nanopore STARD7 repeat counts in the Family 1 patient reflected somatic variation.
checks.evidence_quote: The Oxford Nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats with some interruptions, suggesting somatic variation of repeat sizes may occur within the one individual.

checks.claim: A patient from Family 5 had 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats in STARD7, 4645 bp in total.
checks.evidence_quote: In a second individual (Family 5; III-37), a single Oxford Nanopore read spanned the expanded repeats with 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats; 4645 bp in total length.

checks.claim: FAME patient fibroblasts showed no change in STARD7 mRNA levels.
checks.evidence_quote: showed no significant differences in STARD7 transcript expression in patient-derived fibroblast cell lines (Fig. 3a)

checks.claim: FAME patient fibroblasts showed no change in STARD7 protein levels.
checks.evidence_quote: Protein abundance was also unaltered, confirmed by western blotting using an antibody to STARD7 protein
